If you ever miss streaming, check out Plex. I've got a low data cap and Plex lets me load my own DVDs onto a LAN-accessible desktop and steam them like Netflix.

sup chilly, is there a concise guide anywhere that shows you how to do this? I have loads of DVDs, and ideally would like a server (linux if possible) somewhere in my house that lets me just store them and stream to LAN machines.

Plex has forums that are pretty helpful for first time setup. Usually you'll run three programs: MakeMKV + Handbrake + Plex.

MakeMKV (free) will pull videos off of dvds and blu rays and let you save them on your computer. Handbrake (free, open-source) will convert those videos from MPEG-2 to MP4, which is usually five times more space efficient. Plex (free) is the server software that you install on your desktop; it catalogs your videos, adds movie posters and metadata, and streams them across your LAN with a nice UI. It supports Linux - I've got it running on Fedora - as well as mobile apps and Roku/AndroidTV/AppleTV etc.

Here's a pretty decent setup guide that talks about all three: http://www.maximumpc.com/how-to-set-up-and-use-a-plex-server/

And the three are semi-related: XMBC is the client software that runs on PCs and has some stream-over-LAN functionality. They recently renamed the project to Kodi, so that's the relation there. Plex is a separate software, but because Kodi/XBMC is open-source, the Plex team build their Windows/Linux client using Kodi. Plex Server itself isn't built on Kodi (and I don't think is open-source) and Plex's other clients (Android, iOS, Roku, Xbox, etc) are built natively for those platforms.

If you only watch on PC, Kodi is a good bet and is completely open-source. If you want to watch using a variety of clients (mobile, PC, game console, etc) Plex is a good bet because it has compatible clients for pretty much everything. You can even use Kodi as a front-end for Plex if you don't mind a little tinkering.
